subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how the image got out [Thinking]
passage: In the counsellor Binita's room, Raghav drew arrows on a whiteboard. Tuesday: the picture was sent to one friend. Thursday: it appeared in the group. He pulled out a screenshot, showing which account posted it first, then went quiet. “The first post came from the friend's own phone,” he said slowly. Binita ma'am only asked, “What does that tell you?” Raghav thought aloud. “Not that my friend did it. The phone has no lock, and it stays in the bag at gym time. Someone else could have copied it.” He wrote three lines: tell the friend gently, tell the school with the timeline, and from now on keep private things off any phone that is not locked. Raghav put down the marker. It didn't erase the hurt, but it gave the mess a shape.

qa.q: Where did the first post come from, in the end?
What did Raghav feel when he saw the source of the first post?
qa.a: Shocked and torn: he went quiet, hurt but still wanting to be fair to the friend.

qa.q: What else could Raghav do with this finding, and why?
qa.a: Tell the friend gently so they can lock their phone, since the friend may not know how the picture got out.

qa.q: How might the friend feel when told?
qa.a: The friend may feel guilty and scared, and needs to hear that nobody thinks they did it on purpose.

grounding: A student traces how a picture spread, finds a trusted friend's phone was the source and plans who should be told and how private data is kept safe.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how the image got out [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Pema,
I'm writing because I don't want to say this badly in person, and I don't blame you.
I spent Sunday working out how my birthday photo, the one in my old pyjamas with cake on my face, ended up in the Class Nine group. I sent it to only four people. I checked each forward. The first post in the group came from an account that followed only you and your cousin. When I asked you, you remembered your cousin had your phone all evening at the wedding.
So it wasn't you. It was your phone, unlocked.
Here's what I think we should do. You tell your parents about your cousin. I've already shown Mummy, and she has called our class teacher tonight; they're meeting tomorrow. From now on I'm sending private photos to nobody, and please put a lock on your phone.
Still friends. Always.
Chandrika

qa.q: How many people had Chandrika sent the photo to?
How does Chandrika seem to feel toward Pema in this letter?
qa.a: Chandrika feels hurt by what happened but stays warm and loyal, careful to say there is no blame.

qa.q: What else could the two do to stop this happening again?
qa.a: Pema could keep the phone locked with a code no one else knows, and both could tell a parent at once if anything private leaks again.

qa.q: How might Pema feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Pema may feel guilty and shocked about the cousin, but relieved to be trusted and not blamed.

grounding: Shows a student tracing how a photo spread to a trusted friend's unlocked phone, and using that to plan who to tell and how to keep private data safe.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how the image got out [Thinking]
passage:
Harish, you asked how I figured it out. I'm Jatin, and honestly, I turned detective for a week.
The picture was me in hospital after my cycle accident, face all bandaged. I'd sent it to exactly one person, Kunal, because he's my closest friend. Then it was in a group with “mummy's boy” written on it.
First I was angry at Kunal. But I asked myself: how did it travel? I checked who posted first. It was an account run by kids from Class Seven. Kunal doesn't know anyone there. Then I remembered: his phone backs up to the family tablet, and his little brother is in Class Seven.
So I told Kunal, calmly. He was horrified. We both told our parents that evening; his dad spoke to his brother that same night, and my mum called our class teacher.
Now I only share private things in person. And Kunal turned off that backup.

qa.q: Who had Jatin sent the hospital picture to?
How did Jatin feel at first, and what changed?
qa.a: Jatin was angry at Kunal at first, then calmer after working out how the picture travelled, which turned blame into a plan.

qa.q: What else could Jatin and Kunal do now that they know the source?
qa.a: Check other shared devices and backups at home, and keep private photos off any device someone else can open.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel hearing the explanation?
qa.a: Kunal would feel horrified and guilty that his backup exposed Jatin, but relieved to be told calmly rather than accused.

grounding: Shows a student tracing how a private picture spread to a close friend's phone backup, and using that to decide who to inform and how to keep data safe.
